items.stem: f is continuous and f(1) = −0.4, f(2) = 1.3. What can be concluded?
options: There is no root between 1 and 2
There is at least one root of f(x) = 0 between 1 and 2
There is exactly one root between 1 and 2
items.answer: There is at least one root of f(x) = 0 between 1 and 2
items.markingKey: A continuous function changing sign must cross zero.

items.stem: Explain why f(x) = 1/(x − 2) changes sign between x = 1 and x = 3 but f(x) = 0 has no root there.
items.answer: f has a vertical asymptote (discontinuity) at x = 2, so it jumps from negative to positive without passing through zero; 1/(x − 2) is never 0.
items.markingKey: B1 discontinuity at x = 2; B1 1/(x − 2) ≠ 0 for any x [2]

items.stem: Explain why there may be roots of f(x) = 0 between a and b even when f(a) and f(b) have the same sign.
items.answer: There could be two roots (or a repeated root) in the interval, so the graph crosses the axis twice (or touches it) and returns to the same sign.
items.markingKey: B1 even number of roots or a repeated root; B1 sign returns to the original [2]

items.stem: For f(x) = x² − e^(−x) − 2, f(1) = −1.37 and f(1.5) = 0.0269. Which conclusion is correct?

f(x) = 0 has two roots between 1 and 1.5
f(x) = 0 has a root between 1 and 1.5
f(x) = 0 has no root between 1 and 1.5
items.answer: f(x) = 0 has a root between 1 and 1.5
items.markingKey: f is continuous and changes sign, so there is a root in the interval.

items.stem: Arjun finds that f(x) = (x − 5)²(x + 1) has f(4) = 5 and f(6) = 7, which have the same sign, and concludes that there is no root between 4 and 6. Explain why Arjun is wrong.
items.answer: x = 5 is a repeated root: the graph touches the x-axis at x = 5 without crossing, so f does not change sign even though there is a root in the interval.
items.markingKey: B1 repeated root at x = 5; B1 graph touches without crossing, so no sign change [2]

items.stem: Aisha evaluates f(x) = 5/(x − 4) at x = 3 and x = 5, finds a change of sign and concludes that f(x) = 0 has a root between 3 and 5. Explain why this conclusion is wrong.
items.answer: f is not continuous: it has a vertical asymptote at x = 4, where it jumps from −∞ to +∞. 5/(x − 4) is never zero, so there is no root.
items.markingKey: B1 discontinuity at x = 4; B1 f(x) ≠ 0 for all x [2]
